description: She sailed for Japan in April 1945 with a jet fighter in crates, technical drawings, German experts and about 560 kg of uranium oxide. Germany surrendered while she was in the Atlantic.
fun_fact: Two Japanese officers travelling as passengers took their own lives rather than be captured.
image_credit: Image: Seaman Harry O'Brien · Public domain

name: U-570 (HMS Graph)
fate: Captured in 1941; wrecked on Islay, Scotland, in 1944
description: On her first patrol, with a seasick and barely trained crew, she surfaced beneath an RAF Hudson south of Iceland and was depth-charged. Her captain surrendered to the aircraft.
fun_fact: Commissioned into the Royal Navy as HMS Graph, she made war patrols against her former owners.

name: U-123
fate: Scuttled at Lorient in 1944; raised by France as Blaison; scrapped in 1959
description: In January 1942 Reinhard Hardegen brought her across the Atlantic to open Operation Drumbeat, sinking ships within sight of the American coast.
fun_fact: Hardegen navigated off New York with a tourist guidebook and saw the glow of Manhattan's lights from his bridge.
image_credit: Image: Bundesarchiv, Bild 101II-MW-3983-23 · CC BY-SA 3.0 DE

name: U-977
fate: Surrendered in Argentina in August 1945; sunk as a US Navy target in 1946
description: At sea when Germany surrendered, her captain chose to sail for Argentina. Sixteen men who wanted to go home were landed in Norway; the rest reached Mar del Plata after more than three months.
fun_fact: She spent 66 days of the voyage continuously submerged, breathing through her snorkel.

name: USS Wahoo (SS-238)
fate: Sunk by Japanese aircraft and ships in La Pérouse Strait, 11 October 1943
description: Under Dudley "Mush" Morton she showed the US submarine force how aggressive it could be, sinking some 19 ships in a few months and raiding the Sea of Japan.
fun_fact: She returned from one patrol with a broom lashed to her periscope: a clean sweep. Her wreck was found in 2006.

name: USS Tang (SS-306)
fate: Sunk by her own torpedo in the Formosa Strait on 25 October 1944
description: Richard O'Kane's boat, credited with sinking 33 ships in five patrols, the best record of any American submarine. Her last torpedo ran in a circle and struck her stern.
fun_fact: Some of her crew escaped from the sunken boat 55 metres down using Momsen lungs. Nine men survived, O'Kane among them.

name: USS Barb (SS-220)
fate: Transferred to Italy in 1954; scrapped in 1972
description: Under Eugene Fluckey she sank a carrier, attacked a convoy at anchor in a Chinese harbour and became the first submarine to bombard shore targets with rockets.
fun_fact: In July 1945 eight of her crew paddled ashore on Karafuto and blew up a train. Her battle flag includes a locomotive.

name: USS Cod (SS-224)
fate: Museum ship at Cleveland, Ohio
description: She made seven war patrols in the South China Sea. She is preserved without doors cut in her hull: visitors still climb down the original hatches.
fun_fact: In July 1945 she rescued the whole crew of the stranded Dutch submarine O 19, the only submarine-to-submarine rescue at sea in history.

name: USS Drum (SS-228)
fate: Museum ship at Mobile, Alabama
description: The first Gato-class boat to go to war, in April 1942. She made thirteen patrols and sank fifteen ships.
fun_fact: She is the oldest American fleet submarine still in existence, displayed on land beside the battleship USS Alabama.

name: USS Silversides (SS-236)
fate: Museum ship at Muskegon, Michigan
description: One of the most successful American submarines of the war, credited with sinking 23 ships in fourteen patrols.
fun_fact: In 1942 a pharmacist's mate removed a crewman's appendix on her wardroom table, with spoons bent into retractors, while she lay submerged.

name: USS Pampanito (SS-383)
fate: Museum ship at Fisherman's Wharf, San Francisco
description: She made six patrols in the Pacific. In September 1944 her wolfpack sank Japanese transports that, unknown to them, were carrying Allied prisoners of war.
fun_fact: Returning to the scene days later, she pulled 73 British and Australian survivors from the sea.

name: USS Albacore (SS-218)
fate: Mined off Hokkaido on 7 November 1944
description: At the Battle of the Philippine Sea she fired six torpedoes at the new Japanese carrier Taihō. Only one hit, and her captain was disappointed.
fun_fact: That one torpedo led to the explosion that destroyed Taihō, a result the Navy did not confirm for months. Her wreck was identified in 2023.

name: USS Harder (SS-257)
fate: Sunk by a Japanese escort off Luzon on 24 August 1944
description: Under Sam Dealey she became famous for attacking destroyers head-on. In four days in June 1944 she sank three and damaged others, disrupting Japanese fleet plans.
fun_fact: Her motto was "Hit 'em harder". Her wreck was found off the Philippines in 2024.

name: USS Growler (SS-215)
fate: Lost in the South China Sea in November 1944
description: In February 1943 she collided with a Japanese ship at night and her bridge was swept by gunfire. The wounded captain, Howard Gilmore, ordered: "Take her down!"
fun_fact: Gilmore was left on the bridge so the boat could dive. He was the first submariner to receive the Medal of Honor.

name: USS Tautog (SS-199)
fate: Scrapped in 1960
description: She was at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, where her gunners shot down an attacking aircraft. She went on to make thirteen patrols.
fun_fact: With 26 confirmed sinkings she sank more ships than any other American submarine.

name: USS Nautilus (SS-168)
fate: Scrapped in 1945
description: One of the largest submarines of her day, with two 6-inch deck guns. At Midway she attacked the Japanese carrier force alone, and afterwards specialised in landing raiders and supplies.
fun_fact: In August 1942 she and USS Argonaut carried Carlson's Marine Raiders to attack Makin Atoll.

name: USS Argonaut (SM-1)
fate: Sunk by Japanese destroyers off Rabaul on 10 January 1943
description: The only purpose-built minelaying submarine the US Navy ever had, later converted to carry troops. She was lost with all 102 men after attacking a convoy.
fun_fact: She was the largest submarine the United States built before the nuclear age.

name: USS Darter (SS-227)
fate: Ran aground on Bombay Shoal on 24 October 1944 and abandoned
description: With USS Dace she ambushed the main Japanese force heading for Leyte Gulf, sinking the flagship Atago and crippling the cruiser Takao, and gave the first warning of its approach.
fun_fact: Chasing the damaged Takao that night, she ran hard aground on a reef. Dace rescued her entire crew.

name: USS Torsk (SS-423)
fate: Museum ship at Baltimore, Maryland
description: She arrived in the Pacific in 1945. On 14 August she sank two Japanese coastal defence ships in the Sea of Japan.
fun_fact: Those were the last enemy warships sunk by the US Navy in the war. Hostilities ended the next day.

name: USS Parche (SS-384)
fate: Scrapped in 1970
description: On the night of 31 July 1944 Lawson "Red" Ramage took her on the surface into the middle of a Japanese convoy, firing torpedoes from bow and stern at ranges of a few hundred metres.
fun_fact: "Ramage's Rampage" lasted 46 minutes and earned him the Medal of Honor. Her conning tower is preserved at Pearl Harbor.

name: USS Sealion (SS-315)
fate: Sunk as a target in 1978
description: On 21 November 1944 she torpedoed the battleship Kongō in the Formosa Strait, the only time an American submarine sank a battleship.
fun_fact: One of her crew hung a microphone by the intercom and recorded the attack, a rare sound recording of a submarine in action.

name: USS Grunion (SS-216)
fate: Lost off Kiska in the Aleutian Islands in July 1942
description: On her first patrol she sank two Japanese submarine chasers off the Aleutians and then vanished. Her fate was a mystery for 65 years.
fun_fact: Her captain's three sons organised the search that found her in 2007, with help from a Japanese researcher.
